title: Implement vector bind
description:
Closes #1676.

`bind_rows()` and `bind_cols()` now handle vectors. Vectors are considered to be rows by `bind_rows()` and columns by `bind_cols()`.

The input is preprocessed with `rlang::flatten_if()`, called with a native symbol object containing a pointer to a C-level predicate. This seems to work well and after reading `.Call()`'s implementation, it seems that casting external pointers to function pointers is portable. If you prefer I'll copy `flatten_if()` implementation over to dplyr until the next release.

title: Scoped variants
description:
Scoped variants for:

* `filter()`, closes #2417
* `group_by()`, closes #2053
* `rename()` and `select()`, closes #2120
* `transmute()`, closes #2106

Arguments expecting functions are now more flexible:

* The `.predicate` arguments (for `_if` variants) are passed to `as_function()` (depends on https://github.com/hadley/rlang/pull/77).
* The `.funs` arguments now allow quoted functions (name, quosure) directly (before these had to be wrapped in `funs()`.
* `.funs` is passed both by value and by expression so that named functions can be handled by hybrid evaluation without sacrificing value semantics.
* Anonymous functions are also supported so that `funs()` supports unquoting and `.funs` can be passed a function-valued expression (like `summarise_all(df, identity(mean))`). This has the downside that there's no hybrid evaluation for unnamed functions.

title: Consistent join result when there are rows in right table with no match in left table
description:
This is #2578 take two.

The options are removed, and the important logic is now in `join_vars()`. The list returned by `join_vars()` has a different structure than before: the list (`vars`) contains three parallel character vectors named `alias`, `x`, and `y`. `vars$alias` contains the column names from both tables as they will appear in the join result. `vars$x` contains the names of the corresponding columns in the left table, and `vars$y` contains the names of the corresponding columns in the right table. 

The absence or presence of `NA` values in each position of `vars$x` and `vars$y` is used to indicate which table(s) each column in `vars$alias` should be returned from. If both values in a position are non-`NA` (which happens only in full joins), that triggers a `COALESCE()` in the SQL for that column.

`sql_join.default()` uses a vectorized `paste0()` to create the `select` SQL. It calls three vectorized helper functions which test for the `NA` conditions to determine whether or not to include the different parts of the SQL for each column.

title: Consistent right and outer join results from local and DBI sources
description:
`right_join` and `full_join` currently return discrepant results for SQL sources compared to local data frames when there are rows in the right table with no match in the left table. For local data frames, `by` columns in the join result contain values from the right table for rows from the right table that have no match in the left table.  For SQL sources, `by` columns in the result contain `NA` values for rows from the right table that have no match in the left table.

This pull request provides a resolution to this discrepancy through the addition of a `coalesce` option to `right_join.tbl_lazy` and `full_join.tbl_lazy`. When `coalesce = TRUE`, each `by` column in the result is generated by coalescing the corresponding `by` columns in the left and right tables, using the SQL `COALESCE` function (which is supported by all notable SQL distributions).

Internally, `coalesce` is added to the `by` list in `add_op_join` and then handled in `sql_join.default`. The implementation allows `coalesce` to be specified either as a `logical(1)` or as a `logical` having the same length as `by$x` and `by$y`. The documentation describes only the prior case. In the latter case, each `by` column can be controlled separately.

I defaulted `coalesce = FALSE` for compatibility, but you might consider defaulting it to `TRUE`.

- `funs()` now handles namespaced functions. Fixes #2089.

- depends on an rlang update where literals are not rewrapped on capture → simpler count/tally implementation. Also the last arguments of captured dots are now gobbled by default, which fixes #1039

title: Fix documentation for the `...` parameter in rename/select
description:
## tl;dr

You can't pass a `list()` to `select()`/`rename()`. 

But, the documentation suggests you can. I rephrased the documentation to make it clear a `list()` won't work.

## Longer version

The documentation for the `...` parameter in `select()`/`rename()` parameters begins: 

```r
#' @param ... One or more unquoted expressions separated by commas.
```

But that docstring is incorrect: you can't use R's formal `list()` to pass in multiple unquoted expressions. As evidence, the following are some examples of statements that fail when trying to use `list()`

```r
rename(iris, list(petal_length = Petal.Length))
# Error: All arguments to `rename()` must be named.

rename(iris, list(Petal.Length = petal_length))
# Error: All arguments to `rename()` must be named.

select(iris, list(Petal.Length))
# Error: All select() inputs must resolve to integer column positions.
# The following do not:
# *  list(Petal.Length)

select(iris, list(Petal.Length, Petal.Width))
# Error: All select() inputs must resolve to integer column positions.
# The following do not:
#   *  list(Petal.Length, Petal.Width)
```

title: Make mutate use collecter h
description:
This PR is a continuation to #2486 and closes #1892.

`mutate(col2 = fun(col1))` on a grouped data frame calls `fun` once per group.

It used to require that `fun` returns the exact same type on each call. That is not desirable in functions that may return different (but compatible) types, such as integer and numeric.

This PR changes that behavior, so the returned vectors from each of the `fun` calls are combined using the same coercion rules than `combine` and `bind_rows`, defined in `Collecter.h`.

Comments are welcome. Feel free to be picky, so I can improve a bit my C++ and Rcpp skills. :smiley:

title: Adds mutate support to reference new left-side expressions in lazy-tbl

See https://github.com/hadley/dplyr/issues/2481. This adds support for:

```
df %>% mutate(x1 = x, x2 = x1)
```

Notice that this won't work in `data.frame` nor `lazy-tbl`:

```
df %>% mutate(x2 = x1, x1 = x)
```

title: Prevent the sql optimizer from optimizing empty clauses
description:
While using `add_op_single`, one can define a `SELECT` query that uses `SELECT = c("*")` and no other clause. When this happens, the SQL optimizer in dplyr ends up getting an empty vector during `select_query_clauses` since no other clause is defined. The fix is to only apply the optimization when `outer` and `from` have entries.

The actual repro would be to:

```{r}
install.packages(`sparklyr`)
library(sparklyr)
library(dplyr)

spark_install()
sc <- spark_connect(master = "local")
iris_tbl <- copy_to(sc, iris)
iris_tbl %>% sample_n(10)
spark_disconnect(sc)
```

with output:

```
Error in if (min(outer) > max(inner)) { : 
  missing value where TRUE/FALSE needed
In addition: Warning message:
In max(integer(0), na.rm = FALSE) :
  no non-missing arguments to max; returning -Inf
Called from: sql_optimise.select_query(qry, con = con, ...)
```

title: WIP: A more consistent way to specify query arguments
description:
This defines a class `qspec` with subclasses that provide more control for programmatic use of dplyr verbs. Currently, an example implementation for `select()` is provided. Each verb (or class of verbs) would get its own `qspec` subclass. This solves two problems:

1. Allows passing raw column names or column indexes to `select_()`
2. Simplifies the definition of a consistent API across backends

## Raw column names

Currently, the user can

- use NSE and pass unquoted column names, column indexes, column ranges, selection predicates, etc. in `...`
- use SE and pass quoted column names, quoted column indexes etc. in `...`
- use SE, construct a `lazy_dots` object and pass it to `.dots`

With `qspec` and its `as.qspec_select.character()` and `as.qspec_select.integer()` methods, the user now can also pass named character or integer vectors. (Before, passing character vectors resulted in a call to `parse()`, so that non-syntactic names could not be used directly.)

Passing character vectors also circumvents encoding problems.

The implementation currently addresses #2243 for the `select_if()` case:

```r
> data_frame("a b c" = 1) %>% select_if(TRUE)
  `a b c`
    <dbl>
1       1
```

## Consistent API

For each backend, the implementation of `select_()` basically has to do the same steps:

- call `as.lazy_dots()`
- call `select_vars_()`
- in the grouped case, call `ensure_grouped_vars()`

With `qspec` it is sufficient to call `as.qspec_select()`, and the implementation will figure out what to do, independent of the backend and of the current grouping. This also simplifies future changes/enhancements to the argument processing.

## TODO

- Implement `qspec` for all other verbs
- Use a better name than `qspec`.

@hadley: PTAL.

title: Address issue https://github.com/hadley/dplyr/issues/2302
description:
This pull request should fix issue https://github.com/hadley/dplyr/issues/2302 .

The root cause (as diagnosed by Kirill Müller (krlmlr)) is dplyr SQL was of the form "`a + ('x') IS NULL`" which is potentially ambiguous as to are we checking if `('x')` is null, or checking if `a + ('x')` is null.  Probably this is specified in the SQL grammar- but with at least SQLite it was checking if the overall statement `a + ('x')` is null, which was not the desired behavior in the issue example calculation (and not what the dplyr SQL translator thinks it is emitting).

I have added a test that illustrates the problem, modified another test to accept the new translation, and patched translate-sql-base.r.  I ran check before and after the changes and see no other issues.

I assume the dplyr acceptance suite is much larger than the testthat coverage, so expect more tests will be necessary to accept this pull request.

title: Porting dplyr to c++11
description:
This PR illustrates a minimal set of changes needed to  dplyr c++ to enable C++11 compatibility. All-in-all this was surprisingly little work. @krlmlr and I have discussed the utility of the C++ side of dplyr (the API is very useful, but could be more consistent and stable).

This PR builds cleanly on my OS X box with `clang++`, and all tests pass. You will see warnings if you build against current Rcpp (0.12.7; concerning `##__VA_ARGS__`); these will go away in Rcpp [0.12.7.5](https://github.com/RcppCore/Rcpp/issues/576) There are issues with [`g++` on travis](https://travis-ci.org/jayhesselberth/dplyr); my guess is that these are trivial fixes (e.g. passing correct compiler flags), but someone else could weigh in.

Advantages:

* Removes the dependency on boost (`BH`).
* Future work on dplyr could use C++11 features (`auto` etc).

Disadvantages:

* Would prevent building of `dplyr` with older compilers that don't support the 11 standard.

Other than replacement of boost things  with the equivalent from c++11 `std` (e.g. (`shared/unique_ptrs`, `unordered_map/set`), there are a few other changes:

* `collapse` was renamed to `collapse_string` to prevent a clash with `Rcpp::sugar::collapse()`

* had to define `std::hash<Rcomplex>`. My implementation could probably be improved.

The repo owner only needs to run locally:

``` r
devtools::install_github("ropenscilabs/travis")
```

This does the following:
- registers a new deploy key with the repo on GitHub
- add the encrypted private key to the repo
- install private variables to Travis that allow CI to decrypt the key.

Then, #2206 deploys documentation for each successful build to gh-pages.

I'm planning to use this also to record run time data for benchmarks.

title: Add .dots argument to dplyr::recode to support passing replacements as list
description:
… that they can be saved and reused

`dplyr::recode` and `dplyr::recode_factor` should support a list of replacements with an additional argument such as `.dots`. I know that there are workarounds but supporting this natively would be very useful! Here is an example:

```
x <- c(rep("White", 4), rep("African-American", 2), rep("Hispanic", 2))

dplyr::recode(x, "White" = 1, "African-American" = 2, "Hispanic" = 3)
recode_race <- list("White" = 1, "African-American" = 2, "Hispanic" = 3)
dplyr::recode(x, .dots = recode_race)
```

ps: I think the same would be useful in other "tidyverse" functions (e.g. `dplyr::case_when`, `forcats::fct_recode`). Happy to send a pull request for them as well but first want to see how this goes.

title: Proposing add_count and add_tally for adding an n column within groups
description:
I [very often find myself](https://twitter.com/drob/status/766294758696357888) doing the following three steps (for example, before filtering out all groups below a certain size):

``` r
data %>%
  group_by(...) %>%
  mutate(n = n()) %>%
  ungroup()
```

I've contributed two verbs that shorten this, with working title `add_count` and `add_tally`. They add an `n` column (or an `nn` column if one is already present) to the data frame with counts within groups. Unlike `count` and `tally` the data is otherwise unchanged (same number of observations).

Also included basic unit tests and examples but I can flesh those out more if necessary.

title: Add indirection for src$con
description:
This commit adds `con_acquire` and `con_release` S3 interfaces which dplyr can use when it needs to get a connection from a `src` (instead of just `src$con`). This makes it possible to support connection pools properly; without this change, there is no way for dplyr to signal to a connection pool that it is done with a connection.

Feel free to suggest alternate names for `con_acquire`/`con_release` and their parameters.

I previously had code in `con_acquire.src_sql` and `con_release.src_sql` that detected reentrancy (i.e. `con_acquire` called twice on the same `src_sql` without an intervening `con_release`) and this helped me fix some unit tests. But the reentrancy-detection code was quite messy, so I stripped it before committing. If you prefer to have it in (and perhaps enabled only at unit-test time?) I can certainly add it back.

cc @bborgesr

title: make inner joins explicit to avoid using
description:
@hadley Spark and SQL Server have issues with the `USING` statement and natural joins respectively. This change removes the use of `USING` by making joins explicit at all times. Feedback welcomed. Example follows:

```
library(dplyr)
src <- src_sqlite(tempfile(), create = TRUE)
data_frame(a = 1:3, b = letters[1:3]) %>% copy_to(src, ., "df1")
data_frame(b = letters[1:3], c = letters[24:26]) %>% copy_to(src, ., "df2")
```

Without this PR: `left_join(tbl(src, "df1"), tbl(src, "df2"))`:

```
<SQL> SELECT * FROM 'df1'

LEFT JOIN

'df2'

USING ('b')
```

with this PR: `left_join(tbl(src, "df1"), tbl(src, "df2"))`:

```
SELECT 'a', 'c', 'b.x' AS 'b'
FROM (
   SELECT * FROM 
      (SELECT 'a' AS 'a', 'b' AS 'b.x' FROM 'df1')
   LEFT JOIN
      (SELECT 'b' AS 'b.y', 'c' AS 'c' FROM 'df2')
   ON ('b.x' = 'b.y')
)
```

title: Add select_if() to select based on predicate
description:
This function would be analogous to `summarise_if()` and `mutate_if()`.

One way to distinguish responsibilities between `select()` and `select_if()` is that the former operates on metadata such as the column names, while the latter operates on the columns themselves, and thus requires local sources.

So the custom functions suggested in #1229 would belong to `select()` because they operate on the column names. And more general predicates based on column types (also metadata) compatible with DB sources could be added to `select()`.

Closes #497, closes #1569

title: avoid generating PARTITION BY for empty ones
description:
@hadley: While trying to generate a dplyr partition for this expression for a new backend:

`tbl(db, "flights") %>% filter(min_rank(dep_time) < 2) %>% collect`

the generated SQL was this: 

```
<SQL> SELECT *
FROM (SELECT `year`, `month`, `day`, `dep_time`, `dep_delay`, `arr_time`, `arr_delay`, `carrier`, `tailnum`, `flight`, `origin`, `dest`, `air_time`, `distance`, `hour`, `minute`
FROM (SELECT `year`, `month`, `day`, `dep_time`, `dep_delay`, `arr_time`, `arr_delay`, `carrier`, `tailnum`, `flight`, `origin`, `dest`, `air_time`, `distance`, `hour`, `minute`, rank() OVER (PARTITION BY ORDER BY `dep_time`) AS `zzz4`
FROM `flights`) `mflbvzuway`
WHERE ("zzz4" < 2.0)) `kgbnssdkik`
LIMIT 100000
```

Notice:
1) The `PARTITION BY ORDER BY` clause, this was being caused by, `op_grps.op_base <- function(op) character()` and `order <-` since the group operator is the default and not null. I was not sure if the best fix would be to change the base operator default, but I leaned towards the safer one to scope this to `OVER` sql clauses.
2) Even with the fix for (1), the escaping `"zzz4"` was incorrect, I believe for this one we do need to pass the connection `con` to allow other backends to override the escaping functionality.

Let me know what you think, thanks!

description:
Hello, i tried to use dplyr for my Redshift database with enforced SSL, and the only R library able to connect for me is RPostgres, RPostgreSQL doesn't work for me. I understood from issues i saw that a migration to RPostgres was in order, sorry if i misinterpreted that.

I changed src_postgres to use RPostgres instead of RPostgreSQL and added an additional parameter to copy_to so the BEGIN at the start of the transaction is optional. I added this because for some reason Redshift fails miserably when BEGIN is called, but works flawless otherwise.

I have tried many transformations and this change seems to work fine, though i understand it may break people's code if they are using this assuming it will use the RPostgreSQL driver. If there's a better way to implement this i'll be happy to modify my code per the team's instructions, i'd like to get this upstream for because it'll probably be useful for other redshift users like myself.

Thanks! This R package is magical

title: update the progress bar only 20 times per second
description:
I noticed that RStudio has a high CPU load while running `do` on data frames with many groups and short operations. I traced this to the fact that the progress bar is re-drawn for each tick, even if it hasn't changed since the last update. 

I therefore added a check for when the progress bar has been drawn the last time, and update only if this is more than 50 ms ago. A simple test revealed that this can save a lot of overhead without noticeable changes (first run: normal dplyr, second run: with `last_update` check):

```
> d <- data.frame(x=1:100000)
> system.time(invisible(d %>% group_by(x) %>% do(x=0)))
|==========================================================================================|100% ~0 s remaining        
user  system elapsed
 33.535   2.976  28.715 

Restarting R session...

> library(dplyr)
> system.time(invisible(d %>% group_by(x) %>% do(x=0)))
```

title: Replace indexed-based iteration with more efficient iterator based iteration and pointer arithmetic
description: This is less of true pull request and more of an idea with an example commit. As always comments, critiques, and nit picks are very welcomed! ### Readability I find iterator based iteration to be easier to read and less error prone. ``` c++ // C++11's range-based for loop for(const auto& it : vec) { acc += it; } // is much easier to read and less error prone than the traditional for(int i = 0; i < vec.size(); ++i) { acc += vec[i]; } ``` ### Efficiency Without compiler optimizations and with primitive types iterator based iteration is typically more efficient than index based iteration. For example, the un-optimized pseudo-assembly for loops using iterators would be something like the following ``` x86-assembly leaq 0x0(%rsp), %rcx leaq -0x20(%rsp), %rbx jmp .L2 .L3: /* do work */ subq $0x8, %rcx /* increment */ .L2 cmpl %rcx, %rbx jle .L3 ``` which would be much more efficient than acquiring the offset from the start of the array on each iteration. That being said, the above is probably of no consequence as there is a good chance the compiler optimizations will make this irrelevant. [](https://reviewable.io/reviews/hadley/dplyr/1602)

title: [proposal] ORDER BY in window functions should not be automatically assumed to be also the order of the full final result
description:
### Introduction

When `build_query` generates window functions with `OVER (PARTITION BY x ORDER BY y)`, the query builder then also automatically assumes that not just the partition but also the full final result needs to be ordered by `x` and `y` and thus, inserts an extra `ORDER BY x,y` at the end even though it was never requested. 

Problems with current behavior:
- This creates a significant performance hit for larger queries for no reason. (to the extent that otherwise doable queries become impossible to run). 
- it appears that it is not possible for the user to disable that behavior and remove the offending `ORDER BY x,y` (without modifying the library code).
- this does not appear to be an SQL requirement
### Details

Consider the following test code:

``` r
library(dplyr)

if (!has_lahman("postgres")) {
  stop("You need to have Lahman data installed")
}

salaries <- lahman_postgres() %>% tbl("Salaries")

salaries %>%
  group_by( teamID ) %>%
  arrange( salary ) %>%
  mutate( lower_salary = lag(salary)) %>%
  explain
```

This generates the following query:

```
SELECT "yearID", "teamID", "lgID", "playerID", "salary", "lower_salary"
FROM (SELECT "yearID", "teamID", "lgID", "playerID", "salary", LAG("salary", 1, NULL) OVER (PARTITION BY "teamID" ORDER BY "salary") AS "lower_salary"
FROM "Salaries"
ORDER BY "teamID", "salary") AS "_W1"
```

As can be seen `build_query` adds `ORDER BY "teamID", "salary"` at the end even though it was never specifically requested. 

For large datasets, that could be a large performance hit. As of now, there seems to be no way to disable that behavior.
### Proposed fix

This pull request:
- Disables inheriting the `order by` from inside window functions. (It can always be added by the user explicitly if needed).

For example, with this pull request, the above code produces:

```
SELECT "yearID", "teamID", "lgID", "playerID", "salary", "lower_salary"
FROM (SELECT "yearID", "teamID", "lgID", "playerID", "salary", LAG("salary", 1, NULL) OVER (PARTITION BY "teamID" ORDER BY "salary") AS "lower_salary"
FROM "Salaries") AS "_W1"
```

which is valid SQL and removes the final ORDER BY performance hit

If it is desired to have a particular full final result order, then the users always have the option to specify it explicitly.

``` r
salaries %>%
  group_by( teamID ) %>%
  arrange( salary ) %>%
  mutate( lower_salary = lag(salary)) %>%
  arrange( teamID, salary ) %>%
  explain
```

which generates

``` sql
SELECT "yearID", "teamID", "lgID", "playerID", "salary", "lower_salary"
FROM (SELECT "yearID", "teamID", "lgID", "playerID", "salary", LAG("salary", 1, NULL) OVER (PARTITION BY "teamID" ORDER BY "salary") AS "lower_salary"
FROM "Salaries") AS "_W1"
ORDER BY "teamID", "salary"
```

title: Implemented sql_join for Google BigQuery
description:
Hello everyone! This pull request features an implementation of `sql_join` for "bigquery".

(This is a resubmission of #1220 that I had to close in order to move to a different branch) 
### Motivation

The major motivation for this pull request is that Google BigQuery has powerful SQL join facilities but requires a particular dialect of SQL when doing joins such that regular `sql_join` fails to produce a runnable query.
- Example: SQL keyword "USING" is not supported and the complete column name specification is required. (The default `sql_join.DBIConnection` solution when joining two tables A and B on the common column id is to say  "A JOIN B USING id" while Google BigQuery requires to say "A JOIN B on A.id = B.id")
- Example: Subsequently, Google Query is very sensitive to ambigous names inside SELECT statement and would require one to specify SELECT A.id or SELECT B.id instead of SELECT id which required some change in the logic of `sql_join`.
- Example: When joining large tables "JOIN EACH" keyword is required instead of "JOIN"
### Implementation Details

Some points that are probably worth clarifying for this pull request:
- _Pull request is submitted to dplyr instead of bigrquery_. I thought it is better to submit the pull request to dplyr since the new function heavily mimicks `sql_join.DBIConnection` and relies on pretty much the same non-exported dependencies: `auto_names, unique_names, common_by` etc. 
- _`sql_subquery.bigquery` is modified_. The problem with the current version `sql_subquery.bigquery` that is presented inside `bigrquery` package is that `build_sql` erases "vars" attribute when creating a subquery. However, "vars" are needed for correct subsequent processing of the join. I decided to go with the smallest and safest change possible and just added back "vars" to SQL object.
- only `collect()` works and not `compute()` would work with this pull request. (`compute()` fails due to missing `db_save_query.bigquery` which I submitted as a separate pull request here [hadley/bigrquery#52](https://github.com/hadley/bigrquery/pull/52))
- the function is compatible (and tested) with future `cross_join` that is planned to be implemented as in #197

title: Implemented join for Google BigQuery
description:
Hello everyone! This pull request features an implementation of `sql_join` for "bigquery".

This is my first attempt to contribute to `dplyr` project so I apologize in advance if I am missing some key details (or may be even being overly verbose in describing it)
### Motivation

The major motivation for this pull request is that Google BigQuery has powerful SQL join facilities but requires a particular dialect of SQL when doing joins such that regular `sql_join` fails to produce a runnable query.
- Example: SQL keyword "USING" is not supported and the complete column name specification is required. (The default `sql_join.DBIConnection` solution when joining two tables A and B on the common column id is to say  "A JOIN B USING id" while Google BigQuery requires to say "A JOIN B on A.id = B.id")
- Example: Subsequently, Google Query is very sensitive to ambigous names inside SELECT statement and would require one to specify SELECT A.id or SELECT B.id instead of SELECT id which required some change in the logic of `sql_join`.
- Example: When joining large tables "JOIN EACH" keyword is required instead of "JOIN"
### Implementation Details

Some points that are probably worth clarifying for this pull request:
- _Pull request is submitted to dplyr instead of bigrquery_. I thought it is better to submit the pull request to dplyr since the new function heavily mimicks `sql_join.DBIConnection` and relies on pretty much the same non-exported dependencies: `auto_names, unique_names, common_by` etc. 
- _`sql_subquery.bigquery` is modified_. The problem with the current version `sql_subquery.bigquery` that is presented inside `bigrquery` package is that `build_sql` erases "vars" attribute when creating a subquery. However, "vars" are needed for correct subsequent processing of the join. I decided to go with the smallest and safest change possible and just added back "vars" to SQL object.
- only `collect()` works and not `compute()` would work with this pull request. (`compute()` fails due to missing `db_save_query.bigquery` which I submitted as a separate pull request here [hadley/bigrquery#51](https://github.com/hadley/bigrquery/pull/51))

**Please note** that now there are two different definitions `sql_subquery.bigquery` (one inside `dplyr` and another one inside `bigrquery`). It feels that a better approach is to move `sql_subquery.bigquery` to dplyr as well so it could be closer to `sql_join.bigquery`.

I can submit a separate pull request for moving `sql_subquery.bigquery` out of `bigrquery` to `dplyr` if that solution is found preferable.
### Tests

The code belows demonstrates a test of BigQuery JOIN via dplyr using publicly available data on Google Cloud. Please note that running the test does require to have a Google Cloud billing project set up already. 

The test should run for several seconds and billed for ~9GB of data (~$0.05 USD)

``` r
library(dplyr)
library(bigrquery)

shakespeare <- 
   src_bigquery("publicdata", "samples", billing="<BILLING_PROJECT>") %>% 
   tbl("shakespeare")
wikipedia <- 
   src_bigquery("publicdata", "samples", billing="<BILLING_PROJECT>") %>% 
   tbl("wikipedia")

result <-
  shakespeare %>% 
  select(word, word_count) %>%
  inner_join(wikipedia %>% select(title, num_characters),
             by=c("word"="title")) %>% 
  summarise( n = n(),
             word_count = sum(word_count),
             num_characters = max(num_characters)) %>%
  collect

result
```

title: add parentheses to WHERE clause for complex conditions
description:
When I wrote a code like below, I encountered an unintended result.

``` r
srcs <- temp_srcs("sqlite")
df <- data.frame(x = 1:3, y = 3:1)
tbls <- dplyr:::temp_load(srcs, list(df = df))

temp_tbl <- tbls$sqlite$df
q <- temp_tbl %>% 
  filter(x <= 2) %>%
  filter(x <= 1 || x >= 3)
df <- q %>% collect
df
```

```
  x y
1 1 3
2 3 1
```

The cause is that the `filter` function merely concatenates the conditions.

``` r
q$query
```

```
<Query> SELECT "x", "y"
FROM "offffmlffk"
WHERE "x" <= 2.0 AND "x" <= 1.0 OR "x" >= 3.0
<SQLiteConnection>
```

I expect the WHERE clause to become the below.

```
WHERE ("x" <= 2.0) AND ("x" <= 1.0 OR "x" >= 3.0)
```

title: add mechanism for explicit recycling of columns (#1093)
description:
This PR adds `recycle_each`, and `recycle_whole`, as wrappers over their corresponding `rep` counterparts. A bit of non-standard evaluation sugar is used in `data_frame` to fill in the output length based on the actual resulting number of rows.

The net result is that things like this work:

```
data_frame(x = 1:10, y = recycle_each(1:2), z = recycle_whole(c('a', 'b')))
```

One limitation is that recycled vectors cannot depend on non-recycled vectors, and vice versa. This is a bit of a 'chicken and egg' problem -- in order to recycle a vector, we need to know the number of rows. To figure that out, we need to evaluate every non-recycled vector in the `data_frame` call. And so that evaluation can't depend on evaluation of a `recycle` vector.

title: Allow any number of data frames and lists of dataframes in binding functions

``` r
bind_cols(list(mtcars, mtcars), diamonds)  # diamonds is silently ignored here
```

``` r
bind_rows(mtcars, list(mtcars, mtcars), mtcars)
```

title: Consistent behavior on distinct() when key is set to data.table
description:
Really small change when calling `distinct()` on a data.table with a key.

**Background**

When using a `data.table`, if a key is set, a call to `unique` returns only unique keys, not unique rows. This causes unexpected behavior with `distinct()`:

``` r
> dt_no_key <- data.table(x = rep("a", 4), y = rep(c("f", "g"), 2))
> dt_key <- copy(dt_no_key)
> setkey(dt_key, x)
> dt_no_key %>%
+     distinct()
   x y
1: a f
2: a g
> dt_key %>%
+     distinct()
   x y
1: a f
```

**New behavior**

`distinct()` on a data.table with a key returns unique rows, not just the unique key

``` r
> dt_key %>%
+     distinct()
   x y
1: a f
2: a g
```

title: DOCS: convention to use mtcars.by_vs in group_by
description:
This is a suggestion for a naming convention for variables created with group_by.

I think it would be clearer to use a convention like the following:
    <original tbl name>.<by grouping variable name> 
for naming variables created with group by. 

For example, in the documentation of group_by, mtcars grouped by cyl would be named "mtcars.by_cyl", making it easier to remember which dataset was grouped and how.

If you include this suggestion, the documentation of group_by will be slightly clearer, and maybe more people will use this naming convention for grouped dataset, making the world a slightly better place :-). Otherwise, it will be fine as well. 

There are examples of group_by in dplyr documentation, but since they are included in other functions' documentation, I think it would be more concise to leave them as they are.

title: Speed up Inner Joins in some cases
description:
When using a loop for an inner join, it is best that the LHS table has fewer rows than the RHS table http://msdn.microsoft.com/en-us/library/ms191318.aspx

I've implemented the check on the R side, but it should probably be done at the C++ side (although nrow is generally a cheap operation).  I've also only implemented the generic for dispatch on data.frame arguments, and my test only checks equality, and not column ordering.  That is, if a user specifies the data.frames in a certain order, he/she expects the columns come out in the same order.

Here is an example benchmark of when this matters:

```
x <- data.frame(a = 1:1000, b = runif(1000))
x <- x[sample(nrow(x), 1000, replace = FALSE), ]
y <- data.frame(a =sample(1000000, 1000000, replace = TRUE), d = runif(100000))

inner_join.data.frame1 <- function(x, y, by = NULL, copy = FALSE, ...) {
  if (nrow(x) > nrow(y)) {
    as.data.frame(inner_join(tbl_df(y), x, by = by, copy = copy, ...))
  } else {
    as.data.frame(inner_join(tbl_df(x), y, by = by, copy = copy, ...))
  }
}
inner_join.data.frame <- function (x, y, by = NULL, copy = FALSE, ...) 
{
    as.data.frame(inner_join(tbl_df(x), y, by = by, copy = copy, 
        ...))
}
microbenchmark(
  inner_join(x, y, by = "a"), 
  inner_join(y, x, by = "a"), 
  inner_join.data.frame1(x, y, by = "a"),
  inner_join.data.frame1(y, x, by = "a"),
  times = 20
) -> res

>res
Unit: milliseconds
                                   expr       min        lq    median        uq       max neval
             inner_join(x, y, by = "a")  33.38714  34.93284  35.79604  37.04650  41.51064    20
             inner_join(y, x, by = "a") 747.09208 772.33268 785.33907 796.33719 810.32307    20
 inner_join.data.frame1(x, y, by = "a")  33.93982  35.09669  35.54950  36.87811 180.41901    20
 inner_join.data.frame1(y, x, by = "a")  33.41550  34.48303  35.12243  36.07360  37.58867    20
```

```
> filter( group_by( data, a, b ), x == max(x), b > 2 )

Groups: a, b

  a b x
```
